disease_info: Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features is characterized by at least one full manic episode, often alternating with major depressive episodes, where mood disturbance and changes in energy and activity cause marked impairment or require hospitalization. Manic episodes may include elevated or irritable mood, decreased need for sleep, increased goal-directed activity, and inflated self-esteem or grandiosity, sometimes accompanied by delusions or hallucinations that are typically mood-congruent. Depressive episodes feature persistent low mood and loss of interest, along with biological and cognitive changes, and can be severe, including suicidal ideation. It is distinguished from Bipolar II by the presence of full mania rather than hypomania, and from primary psychotic disorders by the temporal relationship between mood episodes and psychotic symptoms and the persistence of mood symptoms between psychotic breaks.

narrative.personality: Juan is a sociable, hands-on craftsman who thrives on practical problem-solving, community involvement, and creative metalwork projects.
narrative.stressor: In the months leading up to his first clear manic episode, Juan’s shop took on a major new contract that required long hours, tight deadlines, and constant troubleshooting, and he felt personally responsible for keeping the bilingual crew motivated and the client satisfied. He began volunteering for extra shifts, staying late to work on side metal art commissions, and taking on more leadership in community events, leaving him with very little rest and increasing pressure to perform perfectly at work and in the neighborhood. As the weeks went on, this constant overextension and the praise he received for “pulling miracles out of thin air” fed into a growing sense that only he could solve the shop’s problems and that he was destined to expand his work into something far bigger than the job itself, leading to increasingly unrealistic plans and conflicts with supervisors and family over his decisions. The situation escalated when his work quality and reliability started to slip, he clashed with management over safety and project scope, and his family noticed a striking change in his sense of judgment and priorities, prompting his wife and adult children to insist he see a psychiatrist after his behavior jeopardized both the contract and his standing in the community.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I’m realizing now that I started to feel like I was the only one capable of running the whole shop and that I was meant for something much bigger than everyone else seemed to understand.”

narrative.personality: Eva is an outgoing, talkative tech enthusiast who loves teaching others, juggling creative hobbies, and organizing community-focused activities.
narrative.stressor: Around the time she began contemplating transitioning from full-time work to a semi-retired consulting role, Eva found her routine upended by downsizing at her company and an unexpected offer of an early retirement package. Instead of gradually easing into this change, she responded by rapidly filling her schedule with new tech classes at senior centers, additional choir practices, community theater rehearsals, and spontaneous trips to cultural festivals, determined to prove she was entering the “most productive chapter” of her life. Over several weeks, her days became packed from early morning to late night with overlapping commitments and ambitious new projects, and she started taking on responsibilities she couldn’t realistically manage, leaving people confused when she overpromised, double-booked, and became increasingly insistent that she had boundless energy and could do it all. The strain on her relationships, missed appointments with clients, and growing concern from friends at the senior center—who saw her becoming more disorganized and driven in a way that seemed out of character—led her adult daughter to accompany her to a psychiatric evaluation after a particularly chaotic week in which she lost track of basic self-care and work obligations.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I just can’t seem to slow down—I keep starting new projects and signing up for things, and my days are so full I don’t know how to stop.”

narrative.personality: Monika is a disciplined, methodical IT professional who values structure, solitary intellectual pursuits, and steady self-improvement.
narrative.stressor: In the year before her current episode, Monika began experiencing perimenopausal changes and intermittent insomnia, which disrupted the rigid routines she relied on to manage work and personal projects while studying for her ITIL certification. She initially responded by tightening her schedule further—working longer hours, pushing herself to mentor more junior staff, and using late-night study sessions to compensate for feeling less sharp during the day, gradually eroding her sense of balance. After a brief period where she felt unusually driven and confident about her career trajectory despite mounting fatigue, she hit a wall and found herself unable to engage with her usual hobbies—chess, photography, and coding projects—retreating from her social and volunteer activities and struggling to maintain her usual standards at work. The decline in her performance, combined with feedback from colleagues that she seemed unusually withdrawn and unlike her typically precise, engaged self, led her to seek psychiatric help when she realized she no longer cared about activities and goals that had defined her identity for decades.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I’ve lost interest in the things that used to keep me going—my work, my projects, even my hobbies just feel flat and pointless now.”
